name: São Bento Railway Station
short: A Beaux-Arts station designed by José Marques da Silva, whose vestibule carries some 20,000 azulejo tiles by Jorge Colaço depicting scenes from Portuguese history.
long: São Bento station was built on the site of the Benedictine monastery of São Bento de Avé Maria. A provisional station opened in 1896, while the present Beaux-Arts building, with its strong French influence, was designed by the architect José Marques da Silva. Its showpiece is the vestibule, lined with around 20,000 azulejos by Jorge Colaço (1905–1906) showing the Battle of Arcos de Valdevez, the marriage of John I and Philippa of Lancaster, the conquest of Ceuta and the history of transport. São Bento remains one of the city's main transport hubs.
history:
São Bento station was built on the site of the old Benedictine monastery of São Bento de Avé Maria, demolished in the late 19th century. A provisional station opened on 8 November 1896 and was originally called Porto's Central Station. The present Beaux-Arts building, with a pronounced French influence, was designed by the architect José Marques da Silva; work began in 1900.

The vestibule was lined with azulejos by Jorge Colaço: the panels were installed in 1905–1906 and made at the Sacavém factory. Covering some 551 square metres, they number about 20,000 tiles. They depict the tournament at Arcos de Valdevez (1140), Egas Moniz before King Alfonso VII, the entry of John I and Philippa of Lancaster into Porto (1387) and the conquest of Ceuta (1415), along with rural scenes and a frieze on the history of transport that ends with the coming of the railways.

The station was officially inaugurated on 5 October 1916. With its side towers in the manner of the Fontainebleau school, the building is one of the city's principal monuments, and its halls serve not only travellers but also as an exhibition and concert space.

São Bento stands on the Linha do Minho and links Porto with Braga, Guimarães, the Douro line (Régua, Pinhão, Pocinho) and Aveiro. Because it is a terminus, trains enter and leave through tunnels. It has been classified as a monument of public interest (Imóvel de Interesse Público) since 1997.
facts: A provisional station opened on 8 November 1896; the current building was inaugurated on 5 October 1916.
The vestibule holds around 20,000 azulejos covering some 551 square metres.
The panels were made by Jorge Colaço at the Sacavém factory in 1905–1906.
The building's architect was José Marques da Silva.
It stands on the site of the São Bento de Avé Maria monastery.
It has been a monument of public interest since 1997.
Trains run from here to Braga, Guimarães, the Douro line and Aveiro.
tip: Visit the vestibule early in the morning or in the evening, when there are fewer passengers and the light on the tiles is best; entry is free, as it is a working station. The panels are easiest to study from the upper gallery level. The Clérigos tower and the cathedral are a five-minute walk away. São Bento is a metro interchange (lines D and G), handy for getting around the city.
